newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FROM THE HILL-Hard choices facing NZ's Peters.
newsitem.headline: FROM THE HILL-Hard choices facing NZ's Peters.

text.p: Pity Winston Peters -- all the power and a fair slice of the problems.

Saturday's election delivered his nationalist New Zealand First Party the balance of power with 13 percent of the vote. He must now choose to back the ruling conservative National Party or the Labour opposition, and the choices are not trivial.

The election must have been a qualified disappointment for Peters. Early in 1996 the party's support soared to 30 percent on the back of his statements about restricting foreign investment and immigration.
Even when that slipped to the low 20s he was rejecting suggestions he would poll in the mid to high teens as "not even half-right".
But he has emerged with the balance of power -- he calls it balance of responsibility -- and which way he jumps is crucial for his short and long-term game plans.

Looking forward to the 1999 election and beyond, New Zealand First's natural role will be as a nationalist-centrist party or a popular party of the centre right -- the role which has consistently seen National dominate power and the one so effectively taken by Peters' mentor, the late Sir Robert
Muldoon.
If he opts to back Labour he is unlikely to displace it or the Alliance on the left.

If he jumps to the right he can look forward to eventually colonising National (post-Prime Minister Jim Bolger) by forcing the more right-wing elements into the free-market Act New Zealand. Act will take an impotent but inevitably noisy role but together New Zealand First and National can govern without it.

Doing a deal with Labour is on the surface much easier. Their social policies mesh. They both want more spending, oppose bulk funding of schools and reject the competitive model for the health system.

On economic policy there are problems. New Zealand First wants a compulsory superannuation scheme and the second round of tax cuts to go ahead to fund it. Labour wants to defer the cuts and rejig the tax scales so the rich pay more and the poor less. But the problems are not insurmountable and Labour finance spokesman Michael Cullen is working on a compromise solution.

However this similarity itself presents problems to Peters. From National he can wring major concessions and deliver his supporters some trophies. From Labour the best he can hope for is compromise while the Alliance -- whose backing they need -- pulls policy to the left.
By contrast, National can offer a clean arrangement. What it promises, it can deliver.

Then there is the vexed question of New Zealand First's strong Maori support base. National has made much of its previous connections with MPs such as Te Tai Rawhiti's John Delamere, while Peters himself has said the Maori vote has
rejected Labour and so he does not see a reason to take those voters back into coalition with Labour.
Both arguments are disingenuous, although Peters has a reason to promote them to characterise his negotiations with National as a serious option.

Delamere himself points out his row with National over selection procedures ended in court with no love lost. And while all five Maori seats went to New Zealand First on the night, there was still a very strong pro-Labour vote for the party list. If the message was a rejection of Labour's candidates it was not an acceptance of a National government.
Bolger is enthusiastic about the possibility of a deal with good reason -- he is a formidable and flexible negotiator and his leadership of the party may well hinge on him remaining prime minister.

National president Geoff Thompson is equally upbeat, although on election night in Te Kuiti he was more interested in the vain possibility of peeling off some individual left wing MPs to support National.
But there are others in National sceptical of Peters' motives including outgoing trade negotiations minister Philip Burdon, who thinks Peters will talk but nothing will happen.
Their worst nightmare is a major spill in the National leadership and the trading away of important policy planks only to see Peters opt for Labour in the end to humiliate them.
Hints the Employment Contracts Act and the nought to two percent inflation target are on the negotiating table are, to their mind, just the first signs of the damage.

If you wanted to take a punt, the Maori factor and the social policy parallels still favour a deal with Labour. If you took into account Peters' maverick tendencies than a deal short of a full commitment to coalition would draw the smart money.

Whichever way Peters goes it is a safe bet Bolger's poor campaign performance and the push for a rejuvenation of the party will see National go into the 1999 election with a new leader. -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 473 4746
